What was a rocky start has turned into one of the greatest looter/shooters on the market.



Pros

Gunplay: Seriously, this is the greatest implementation of a cover based shooter ever designed. Ability to move from cover to cover, lay down supressive fire, and assault your enemies in a tactical mindset is amazing. Just don't expect much if you're grouping with randoms.

Story: Not great, but not to bad either. Your classic Tom Clancy fair of military storytelling. Take points and things from our actualy reality and embelish certain elements to craft a fine experience.

Immersion: This is top notch in this game. The atmosphere as you travel down forgotten hallways, ramshackled streets and especially the body filled zones of Central Park all help nhance the experience of surviving an epidemic.

Gear: The amount of gear combos is daunting at first, but with well established sets, easy to follow stats, and the ability to swap not only gear, but abilities on the fly gives you multiple ways to play the game any way you wish.

Survival: the survival mode (DLC) is one of the few gaems which still tends to surprise me from time to time. Every mission has 'nail bitting' moments where survival is always in question. A great edition to the game and one of my favorite modes it has.

Cons

This is an RPG first and a shooter second. Even though the shooter/cover mechanics are amazing at its core this was designed to be an RPG style game. Enemies take multiple rounds (sometimes even magazines) to fall. Don't come into it expecting one bullet, one kill.

SOme DLC is questionable. While I deeply enjoyed the underground gameplay/grind, it was a pretty lame expansion to charge people for. While the randomly generated missions can give you some fantastic moments, it should have been free more than likely.

The Age: Game has been out for awhile. If you're coming in now, you'll be slightly behind the curve. Catching up isn't overly difficult (the game throws gear at you like candy) but expect the fiorst 10-20 hours to be a catch up game.

Raids: I love them, but they are some difficult combat scenarios, which turn alot of people away. Don't expect to waltz in like you do for other missions and clear it with a bunch of randoms watching tv as the play. It will test you. Finding a good group to consistenlty play with will help.

PvP: this is both a blessing and a curse. Sometimes in the Dark Zone you will have epic PvP battles intermingled with the doubt that the approaching player will or will not shoot you in the back. Waiting those last 20 seconds for an extraction to get out of the zone with your loot can end in triumph or despair. For some this can be a turn off. I enjoy it. It also possesses 4v4 'battlegrounds' which I havent stepped into ever.  PvP will happen, but for some that may not be a good thing.

Overall, The Division is a game which I have had zero regret about sticking with. I'm looking forward to its sequel and the improvements Massive will bring with it.

I'll be honest - the only thing that keeps me hooked on this game is the atmosphere. That snowy, desolate New York City is absolutely breathtaking. The visuals, the sound design, the little stories told through abandoned apartments and scattered notes... it's pure immersion. And the music? Man, that song on the radio, "Gone to Sleep," is absolutely perfect for this world. It's haunting, emotional, and fits the mood of a city falling apart perfectly. That track alone got me every single time it played.

The mission design, though? Classic "go here, grab that, come back" routine. Lazy and repetitive.

But here's what really stings. This game is basically dead now. The online population is tiny, and finding random teammates is next to impossible. I don't have any friends to squad up with, so I went in solo, fully knowing what I was getting into. And let me tell you, it's rough. Enemies are bullet sponges, you get swarmed constantly, and the difficulty is clearly balanced for a full team. Playing alone feels like an uphill battle from start to finish.

And yet, despite all that, I actually love this game. I keep coming back to it. Not for the quests, not for the combat, but for that world and that music. They pull me in every time, no matter how frustrating the rest gets. Yeah, I suffer through it, but somehow I still enjoy the ride.

I bought this game during this 2018 Summer Sale. I'm going to assume you know what The Division is. I'm going to assume that you understand the issues it had early on. I'm going to assume you're just wanting an honest review of if it is worth the money now.

And I'd have to say yes. I picked up the Gold edition while it was on sale, under $20. It's everything that I expected it to be knowing it had been fixed up, and then some. The combat isn't the most exhilarating, shooting the same enemies with a full mag over and over can get a little monotonous, but it's still pretty fun, especially with another teammate or 3. The abilities and different weapons do a good job at keeping the game fresh, even if you're sometimes just swapping out a G36 for a better G36. 

The thing that really sets this game apart from others, and made me want to write a review, is the setting and atmosphere. NYC is an absolute blast to run around in, see the different people, find more clues to fill in the story, etc. I've found myself sitting in a Safe House, listening to the announcer on the radio telling people what's going on with absolutely fantastic voice acting to back it up. You seriously feel like you're in NYC when a massive outbreak happened. Everything is insanely believable. The overall main story may be a little "meh," but the clues, recordings, scene recreations (called ECHOs) CCTV Camera recordings, and other pickups completely fill in what's left to be desired. Listening to a phone call from a husband telling his wife to pack up NOW, with little explanation as to why from his end, is very believable, and fairly chilling. 

I can wholeheartedly say, this game is the most immersive game I've played. The setting is absolutely top notch, and I feel is something that everybody should experience.

I do get some frame dips here and there, which shouldn't necessarily happen on my build, but it's not something that hinders the gameplay too much. The gunplay is also pretty realistic. There's nothing like shooting an enemy through the windshield of a car, and watching the glass splinter and shard outwards in a realistic way.

If you have any reservation on this game, I'd say pick it up in the next sale. I have not gotten around to playing the other two game modes, Survival and Last Stand, but I've heard good things about them. I'm just too engrossed in the singleplayer portion of the game to have even entered the Dark Zone yet. Give it a try, test out the atmosphere, start upgrading your character, and I really don't think you'll be disappointed.

So I was super late on picking up the Division 1 but I did so right before the release of the Division 2 and after putting close to 500 hours in that, I'd say that gives me a pretty good stand on comparing the two games. Ultimately, I'm going to lean more towards the first game as it plays somewhat superior to the second game, not mechanically so much, but in a way that makes the gameplay loop satisfying and replayable. 

While the missions aren't as cinematic, long, or as diverse as the Division 2's, they're still pretty good and I like them for what they're worth. They're very grounded and not over the top with action packed sets or ludicrous stories. I'm not going to say they're better in pretty much any aspect but I did enjoy them enough. They're all pretty replayable which is nice because in Div2, you either loved a mission or you hated it. For example, I HATED the presidential bunker mission because it dragged on forever and was pretty boring but I loved the American History Museum because it was fun. In Div1, the missions were mostly average but likeable. 

So the Dark Zone in this game is far superior to the ones in the second game. For whatever reason, Massive opted for 3 separate and compressed Dark Zones for what I can only imagine was to force more PvP encounters. This absolutely sucked because you could fast travel to different checkpoints to quickly catch up and not to mention that they have 3 evac area (started with 2) which meant you were almost always being stalked which made getting farmed items a bitch. At least in this one, you could take routes to purposely avoid conflict and sneak your stuff away mostly unbothered. Don't know why they decided to make the Dark Zone in Div2 a mostly PvP affair. It's also what basically killed balance in the second game as in Div1, your build was as strong as you made it. In the Div2, they balanced the PvP so much that it ultimately destroyed the game as exotics were getting nerfed and sets made useless so your builds were gambles as to whether or not they'd be nerfed. I had a super seeker build for PvE that got utterly destroyed and made all my effort for that build worthless. Also, I liked the feel of the massive Dark Zone in Div1 a whole lot more, it felt like this abandoned hell that was just overtaken, the ones in Div2 felt the same way but they just lacked that same feeling.

So the gameplay mechanics are where Div1 shows both an advantage and disadvantage. In the Div2, the gunplay are overall controls were much better, there's absolutely no disputing that. But after all the patches the Div1 got, the devs found the sweet spot, they simplified everything which ultimately made the game much less of a hassle. In the Div2, everything just became so muddled and messy. Div1 gave you your power fantasy and let you feel powerful when you equipped yourself properly while Div2 felt like an eternity of min/maxing which never paid off. In short terms, while they improved the game mechanically, they made everything else so damn messy that it just took away from the fun. While 1-30 in Div1 was awful while the endgame was amazing, it was the exact opposite in Div2.

Now Post Launch support is where these games have a huge difference, we are now at the 2 year mark of Division 2's release and well, the post launch support it has received at this point is abysmal. Summed up by broken and buggy releases, greedy seasons, and an overall lack of community interaction on Massive's part. Div1 delivered a phenomenal turn around with some of the best DLC, specifically Underground, bringing Div1 to the great state it is currently in while Div2 sits in a puddle of disappointment of constant community dissatisfaction from broken promises and undelivered content. They undersold the Div1 and added on with great content later on while the Div2 entirely oversold itself post launch roadmap.

Nitpicks: These are some of my nitpicks on what makes the Div1 a much better game
- Cosmetics are much better looking in this game
- Factions are more grounded in their setting and less kooky than their Div2 counterparts, they belong to their world
- New York has a much better atmosphere than D.C, something about the dark and desolate streets of NY as well as the world feeling more alive
- The builds are simplified so it doesnt feel like you have sit down and calculate your new potential builds
- Base of Operations was SO much better than the white house (screw that alarm) and 2 communities, like with DZ, it just felt like they disjointed your entire BoO and split it into 3 areas while giving much less charm.
- More memorable characters than the Div2, god, this game had much better characters, the ones in the Div2 were just not great
- Facial animations, just look at the difference in the games. They're not perfect here but theyre still better
- The graphics hold up REALLY well for it's age
- More interiors in NY so exploring feels a little more satisfying as every open window and door attracts attention
- Story was pulled off better. While neither game had a great story, Div1 pulled it off better, kept it simple and forward moving while Div2 threw way too much exposition your way.
- Sound design was better, the ambience of walking down the streets down to the gun sounds themselves, for some reason, they made gun sounds in Div2 sound like pop guns.
- More replayable content.
- Much better endgame loop.
- Mostly bug free
- Not riddled with these new "seasons" which were basically designed to make people spend money, in other words, no half-assed battlepasses and no half-assed events with recycled rewards with ridiculous grinds
- Grinding feels much less tedious

Overall, even if the Div2 is a slightly more mechanically better game, the Division 1 has come back to the top simply because the devs mishandled the living hell out of Div2. Hell, Div1 still has a pretty active playerbase so you wont have much issue finding games. They did right by Div1 up until 1.8, the game is in a great state, however, it's like they brought Div1 back from the grave and then gave us the Div2 then slowly pushed that into an early grave.

TL;DR Ubisoft brought an amazing concept to the world, and once again didn't listen to it's fan-base. And so, the game fell to ruin, thanks to lack of anti-cheat and rampant hacking in PvP.

Also, the amount of hours posted does not reflect actual hours played. I owned this game through uPlay before migrating to Steam.

Now, the actual long part:

Surprisingly enough, the PvE is plenty fun and challenging enough, for a while. Typical copy/paste fetch quests, area defense, and assassination targets. The forgettable story is crappily stapled on to the endless grind to reach level 30. After that, there are plenty challenging daily missions and other repeat missions for higher quality loot, which is all fine and dandy until you decide that it's not enough.

Then you go to the Dark Zone, or DZ for short. DZ is the part where they royally messed up. The DZ has it's own currency, it's own ranking system, and it's own rules. To start off, the DZ has it's own ranking system separate from single player. The level cap is much higher, and the quality of loot increases with each level. The trick is, you have to visit the DZ every few single player levels to rank up your DZ rank so you aren't completely out-geared and out-matched by the time you hit rank 30 outside the DZ. Not fun, and not well thought out. Especially considering if you die in the DZ, you lose a few DZ levels.

Second is the currency. Forget all that money you've been earning through your single player experience. DZ only takes DZ credits in exchange for getting DZ quality gear. Only way to get DZ credits is by slaying mobs in the DZ. Should you find yourself dead in the DZ, you lose a portion of your DZ credits, far more than you'd earn in a simple run through the fastest mob routes. So profit is tough, especially if you're under-leveled. Don't let that get you down, because if you want high quality gear without the DZ, there's always the dailies and weeklies you can beat to earn yet ANOTHER type of currency to use back at the home base. But not to buy good weapons, just the blueprints. You gotta craft the weapons, and hope you get the stats and skills you want on it.

Now for the grand scheme. Take the levels, the currency, and add in PvP. PvP is possible in the DZ, but you get "punished" for doing so. Killing players or stealing loot will mark you as a rogue agent for a short duration, will put a bounty on your head, and make you visible to all other players in your vicinity. If you can live through the timer, you get the bounty, if you get killed, your killer gets the bounty. The more players you kill in a short span, the higher the bounty and the longer the timer. Pretty fun and fair for all. Except, it's not. Thanks to a near-non-existant anti-cheat system, the DZ is rife with players using hacks and exploits to simply ruin other's days. Mix that in with trying to earn DZ levels and DZ credits, and your in for a lot of profit loss.

The worst part, after all of that, is Ubisoft doesn't care. Not like it's anything new, but this really takes the cake. Ubisoft, deaf to the aguish and cries of the users, continues on it's merry little path of getting out all it's "Year One" content. Patches, bug fixes, adding in new missions, new currencies that we can't keep track of, new gear, guns, and much, much more, and yet, no anti-cheat. No help for those who thought this game was a much needed change from the pace of rinse-and-repeat First Person Shooters. I can only pray they don't let For Honor fall into the same pit of despair that they have The Division.

(P.S. Hey, Ubisoft, if you're reading this, you should add BattlEye to The Division like you did Siege. It's kinda helping.)

I've taken three swings at this game on PC and Xbox over the years.  Most recently, I picked it up again on PC and played through to the end game before writing this review.

I'm friendly to this sort of over-the-shoulder presentation, other than when the camera fails and I can't see my target but only my own back. ;-)  I'm a play-the-story and run-all-the-side-quests kind of completionist.  If you're not, then some of my commentary won't be as useful.  Stipulating that, there's LOTS to complete in this game and that's very fulfilling.

I like the leveling in the game and found, personally, that running all the side quests and maybe replaying some of the mission content on a harder level let me level up my character "ahead of the map".  This let me spend more time enjoying engagements and running the map rather than worrying about dying all the time. I'm not a Dark Souls fan for this very reason.  Again, Your Mileage May Vary.

I find the combat model to be solid, predictable, crisp.  You need a decent graphics card and plenty of RAM to keep the model feeling crisp.  This is a shoot-from-cover game.  No toe-to-toe, hack-and-slash battles here.  On the PC keyboard, movement control in battle, ESPECIALLY while retreating, can be hit-or-miss (please pardon the pun).  My greatest frustrations in the game have been trying to correctly control the keyboard while in retreat.  I often have troubles with the move out of cover walking instead of running, missing the next cover point, or landing on a cover point that is still exposed and having to force the character around the corner.  Lots of dying there.  This may be because I suck at keyboard control.  Could be.  I don't recall having this much trouble in similar situations on the Xbox, which suggests either failing memory or finding the controller easier to navigate than the keyboard in those scenarios.  YMMV.

Interactions with the world are pretty reliable with some minor annoyance from some items that are in field-of-view aren't recognized as actionable. Usually this happens when I'm standing too close to the item.  Not a big deal, but it breaks the flow when you're moving quickly around the map.

I'm VERY happy with the gearing improvements that come at Level 30 as you enter end-game.  I immediately picked up a series of great high-end gear that changed game play for the better.  I was really worried about being tough enough for end-game and wasn't looking forward to the anticipated gear-grind that one sees in, say, Destiny or most RPGs.

Which brings me to the Dead Zone.  I've hated the Dead Zone in the past.  It's just too damn hard.  Yeah, great reward from great risk and all that.  I get it.  But going back and forth between the story line and the Dead Zone never worked for me.  I hit it a couple times coming up through the ranks this play through and it was better than I remembered.  I first journeyed in around L19.  Given the end-game gear and my wildly-improved toughness, I'm ready to give it another try.

Ultimately, this is a really good game.  I enjoyed playing through The Division 2, which I never end-gamed, either.  But this is a solid franchise that provides many hours of enjoyment even for a fairly conservative battle-at-a-distance sort of game play.  And it's an adrenaline rush when you have a skilled run pushing against enemies.  Highly recommended.

[h1] The Game that made me fell in love with Online-only Multiplayer Genre:	[/h1]
Tom Clancy's The Division is an action role-playing video game. It is set in New York City in the aftermath of a smallpox pandemic; the player, a Special Agent of the Strategic Homeland Division which is named as the  "Division", is tasked with helping the government maintain order and control over the Manhattan, investigate the nature of the outbreak, and combat criminal activity.

[h1] Gameplay:	[/h1]
The game is played in third-person perspective. As the player progress they earn experience points and currency which is used to buy items and upgrade the player's character. The crafting mechanism allows to craft weapons,upgrade existing items. In this game you basically fight enemies to get a better item than the one which you currently possess. The enemies difficulty level are based on level based system. This review is based on 100% completion and 111.4 hours of gameplay.

[h1][b]Recommendation:[/b][/h1]
Would I recommend this game? Absolutely.

I've been a fan since its Xbox release and recently picked it up on Steam. While the player base is smaller than it once was, it’s still an amazing experience. Some modes, like full lobbies in Survival, Strike [i](PvP)[/i], and other group activities, can be difficult—if not impossible—to find games for, but a small, loyal community keeps the game alive.

What really draws me in is the well-crafted story and atmosphere—it’s a masterclass in world-building. This is one of the few games with a realistic, gritty narrative that doesn’t feel far-fetched and seems like something that could actually happen. That extra layer of believability makes it even more immersive. While the graphics may feel a little dated compared to its sequel or newer titles, the art direction and style more than make up for it. In fact, I personally think this game has a stronger narrative and visual identity than The [i]Division 2.[/i] Those two aspects alone make it worth playing.

The gameplay and gunplay still hold up today. While [i]The Division 2[/i] refines many mechanics, combat remains fun and satisfying. The key is optimising your build—without good gear, enemies can feel like bullet sponges. But once you’ve got a solid setup, the combat becomes much more rewarding.

PvP isn’t really my thing, so I only played enough for the achievements. In the Dark Zone, you’ll either find no one [i](due to the small player base)[/i] or run into fully optimised players who’ll melt you. That said, it’s still fun—even when getting destroyed by a Russian guy on proximity chat saying, [i]"Please brotha, heal brotha. Good job brotha."[/i] Like the rest of the game, it’s best with others, but the low player count makes it far less active than it used to be.

One of the biggest downsides is the near non-existent matchmaking. I struggled to find players for any mission or mode. While a small, dedicated player base remains, I rarely saw others in the Dark Zone or Survival and only a handful in the main hubs. If you want a team, your best bet is to organise one outside the game or hope to run into someone to invite.

Now onto the DLC, which I personally wasn’t a fan of.[list]

    [*]Underground is a massive grind with little reward. Missions consist of 1–3 randomly generated phases, each taking at least 15 minutes. Levelling is painfully slow, and the limited tile sets make the gameplay feel repetitive fast. After a few runs, you’ve seen it all, making the mode a complete time sink with minimal payoff.

    [*]Survival is slightly better—not a mode I enjoy, but I’ll give them credit for trying something fresh. I only played PvE for achievements, but PvP works like the Dark Zone with survival extraction mechanics added. The difficulty can be brutal, and playing with one other person is highly recommended. Full squads might struggle due to limited resource sharing. Interesting concept, but not for me.

    [*]Last Stand [i](PvP)[/i] was also a complete miss. The mode is completely dead, so I couldn’t find a single game. Worse still, the DLC adds unskippable dialogue every time you visit the Terminal, and the only way to remove it is by playing a PvP mode that you can’t find a match for. Not worth it.[/list]

Despite its age and a small but dedicated player base, [i]The Division[/i] is still 100% worth picking up—at least for the base game. I strongly recommend getting it on sale, as it frequently gets discounted. Unless you’re going for 100% completion, the DLC isn’t worth it.

[h1][b]Achievements:[/b][/h1]
Recently, Steam achievements were added to the game. If you’ve played before and already met the requirements, they will unlock retroactively.

[i][b]At the time of this review, Last Stand DLC achievements haven’t been added, which is a good thing since the mode is dead.

DLC is required for 100% completion, with multiple co-op, multiplayer, and PvP achievements.[/b][/i]

The good news is that all achievements are unmissable and can be completed at any time, so you can play at your own pace and clean up anything later. Since Steam doesn’t have a dedicated achievement guide yet, I highly recommend using TrueAchievements. That said, a guide isn’t essential, as most unlock naturally. If you complete everything as you go, by the time you reach endgame, you should only have a few things left to mop up before tackling the DLC.

Collectibles are extremely easy to get. There’s a perk in the Base of Operations [i](BoO)[/i] that reveals all collectibles on the map for a completed area. I recommend leaving collectibles until the end and just picking up any you happen to find naturally along the way.

The main ones to watch out for are the PvP achievements in the Dark Zone. If possible, boost these with another player, as you’ll likely run into people with fully optimised builds. You’ll also need to extract at all 8 different extraction zones in DZ01 – DZ06, and having another player helps a lot. We only ran into one other player while doing this, but if you’re struggling, try:[list]

    [*]Playing during off-peak hours

    [*]Lowering your gear score [i](if max level)[/i] to get placed in a lower bracket

    [*]Starting a fresh character

    [*]Completing these achievements during the levelling process[/list]

Unfortunately, there’s no guaranteed way to avoid getting wrecked by other players—you’ll just need some luck and/or skill.

Underground is a massive grind, especially if you play solo. You’ll need to reach max level (40) and run at least 80 phases to get all collectibles. If possible, find a high-level host, as they can apply more modifiers to speed up XP farming. For collectibles, you’ll only ever find one per phase—usually at the start or halfway through—so don’t waste time searching in combat areas. You’ll also need to finish a game with 3 other players while the host is level 30 and has all modifiers enabled.

Survival is brutal. You can queue for up to 6 minutes, and as long as one person is in the queue, the match will start. I highly recommend playing in PvE, even though PvP gives more XP—you’ll already get more than enough XP in PvE, so only play PvP if you enjoy it or want the challenge.

The Hoarder achievement requires 17 successful extractions with all 6 loot slots filled. This is the real grind—each run takes 40+ minutes, and if you die, that’s 40 minutes wasted. Playing with another person is highly recommended, as a teammate massively improves your survival chances. Unlike Underground, where XP accumulates over multiple runs, the Survival XP achievement is based on a single run’s rating. This means you can unlock it in one go if you score high enough by surviving longer, extracting with better loot, and securing high-value items etc.

A big tip for Survival mode is to use a sniper as your primary weapon and anything else as your secondary—the G36 assault rifle is a solid choice. When extracting, use the big area in the middle of the Dark Zone [i](DZ03)[/i], then head into the back corner building and use that as your spot to take down Hunters. This makes dealing with them much easier.

The biggest tip I can give for PvP-related achievements or gameplay:

Trust [b]NO ONE.[/b]

Many players will try to mess you up or grief you, so only trust yourself or a premade team—just focus on what you need to do.

Overall, while many achievements are easy, the co-op and PvP ones can be a pain, and Survival and Underground require a serious grind. If you’re going for 100%, be prepared to put in the time—but if you boost with others, it’s more than manageable.

This game (All though I am a traditional MMO fan. WoW and such.) is a MMO like Destiny. 
Has a loot system similar to Diablo/Borderlands. 
Completely gear dependent/driven scaling mechanics.
Yes, there is bullet sponging; like any other MMO out there.
Yes, its core mechanics will end up being repetitive; like any other MMO out there.

Overall, The Division gives us a fresh take on what we consider MMORPG. 
The use of Third Person, Cover Based shooting hasn't been done in a RPG feel. The Division does a excellent job in providing for that mechanic throughout it's various encounters and PvP zones.

I will advise that people who expect this game to be like CoD, CS:GO, or GOW will not have a very enjoyable time.
You cannot just start running into a group of 5 to 10 NPCs and expect to win. 
You cannot come into the game and expect to take on Players or NPCS high level than you with ease.
This game is a time sink; meaning that you are required to put some playtime down to get to the point of dominating the majority of challenges in this game.
You have to work, craft, and tweak your gear to specific play styles and talent/ability builds to fully maximize your usefulness in combat. You can't run in with a bunch of green items and be on a level playing field with somebody with blue items who has reconfigured the stats to maximize their damage with weapon or skill.
You can expect to unload FULL CLIPS into people's heads and not kill them if you don't play this game like an MMORPG.

I've played The Division in the last two betas along with launch. This game has HUGE potential to be a great game.
The story is great. The challenges are fun and can be difficult. Playing with a group (of 4) maximizes the chaos and entertainment in the game. Challenges scale with group size.

If you want a Third Person Cover Based MMORPG, this is a game for you.
You want a game to play with friends and enjoy working together, this is a game for you.

If you want to run around trying to 360 no scope headshot people, this game is not for you.
If your looking for a action shooter that involves W+M1 or just running and gunning, this game is not for you.
